Link the Joseph Pratt household in the 1860 and 1880 Salt Lake County, Utah census records (src_001 and src_002) to the right people in the tree.

No warnings. The tree is clean.

---

Both census households have been matched to the right tree persons, and the facts from both records are now written onto the tree. Every name, birth year, birthplace, and residence the censuses record has been added to Joseph, Ann, Sarah, and young Joseph — all still born in England, all living in Salt Lake County, Utah by 1860 and again in 1880.

The 1860 census shows the whole family intact: Joseph Pratt (head, born about 1822 England), his wife Ann (born about 1825), their daughter Sarah (born about 1847), and their son Joseph Jr (born about 1850) — every one matched with high confidence to the corresponding tree person. The 1880 census confirms Joseph and Ann are still in Salt Lake County twenty years later, now with son Joseph Jr (age 30) still living with them. Sarah is absent from the 1880 record; she was likely married and living elsewhere by then, or possibly had died — that gap is worth following up.

The move from Bedfordshire, England to Utah is fully accounted for: the FamilySearch Utah Emigration page confirms that Latter-day Saint converts from Great Britain emigrated in large numbers to Utah from 1855 onward, sailing from Liverpool to American east-coast ports. No further source is needed to accept the Utah residence as plausible for this English family. The next productive step would be to search for a marriage record for Sarah Pratt (last seen in 1860, age 13, so marriageable by the mid-1860s) and to look for passenger or pioneer records documenting the family's actual crossing from England, which would close the pre-1860 gap and directly answer the project's guiding question.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

output.text_response:
**Review: pe_005 (a_013 → I1, Patrick Flynn)**

---

**What the entry records**

pe_005 links assertion a_013 to Patrick Flynn (I1) at `confident`. a_013 is a `relationship` fact-type assertion from the 1908 Schuylkill County death certificate, stating "Father: Thomas Flynn." Its informant is James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law, with `information_quality: secondary` and `informant_proximity: family_not_present`.

---

**The full death certificate context**

The same record produced three assertions:
- **a_011** — Death fact ("12 March 1908, Schuylkill County") — primary information, attending physician.
- **a_012** — Birth fact ("Born 1845, Pennsylvania") — secondary, from the son-in-law; a direct conflict is noted (the certificate says Pennsylvania, but census records say Ireland).
- **a_013** — Relationship ("Father: Thomas Flynn") — secondary, same son-in-law.

Of these three, only a_013 is linked to I1 via pe_005. a_011 and a_012 carry no pe_ entry pointing to I1.

---

**Assessment of the confidence tier**

The `confident` tier for the identity pairing is **defensible on the underlying merits.** Patrick Flynn dying in Schuylkill County in 1908 and naming Thomas Flynn as father maps cleanly onto a tree person already placed in that county under Thomas Flynn's household in both the 1850 and 1860 censuses (pe_001, pe_004). That convergence of name, location, year, and family position is a strong-to-obvious identity match. The tier itself is not miscalibrated.

However, the rationale has **four distinct deficiencies** that make it inadequate to support that tier on its face:

1. **Missing required check lines.** The rationale should open with a "Date check:" line (record birth year vs. tree person birth year) and a "Residence check:" line (record place/year vs. nearest attested residence). Neither is present, making the entry unauditable.

2. **No match_score disclosure.** The field is null with no explanation. For a tree person already present with source refs, `same_person` should have been called, or the rationale should explain why it was not.

3. **The informant's reliability problem is unaddressed.** James Brown is a son-in-law who was not present at birth and demonstrably reported Patrick's birthplace incorrectly (Pennsylvania vs. Ireland, per a_012's extraction note). This doesn't cap the identity tier, but it must be acknowledged so reviewers understand what weight a_013 actually carries.

4. **The rationale conflates a_011 with a_013.** The text describes "names match, death location matches known residence" — which describes the *death fact* (a_011), not the *paternity assertion* (a_013) being linked. Using one assertion's identity anchor to justify linking a different assertion is a subtle but real flaw.

---

**Summary**

The `confident` tier is not wrong given the converging census evidence (pe_001, pe_004), but the rationale as written does not demonstrate that case. It omits the required check lines, discloses no match score, ignores the informant's known weakness, and conflates the death-fact anchor with the relationship assertion being linked. A reviewer encountering pe_005 in isolation could not audit it.

---

**Recommended corrective action**

An updated rationale should:
- Add **Date check**: "Birth year ~1845 on certificate vs. ~1845 in tree: gap 0 years."
- Add **Residence check**: "Schuylkill County, PA, 1908 vs. Schuylkill County, PA (1860 census, pe_004): same."
- State why `same_person` was not called, or call it and record the result.
- Note the informant's birthplace discrepancy (a_012) while clarifying that identity rests on name + location + the Thomas Flynn father link — not on the informant's secondary parentage report.
- Clarify that the identity anchor comes from a_011; a_013 specifically contributes the *parentage claim* behind q_001.

Would you like me to draft the improved rationale text and update pe_005?

Here is the subagent's full report:

---

**Correlation analysis — 1875 census "Anders Pedersen" (a_001) vs. I1 (Anders Hansen)**

**Points of agreement:**
- Given name "Anders" — exact match
- Birth year ~1868 — exact match
- Birthplace Ringsaker, Hedmark, Norway — exact match

**Core identifier conflict:**
The patronymic surname "Pedersen" means "son of Peder." The tree person I1 is "Anders **Hansen**" — "son of Hans" — with father recorded as Hans Olsen (I2). These are different names: Peder ≠ Hans. Norway's patronymic naming system was still in active use in 1875 (fixed surnames were not mandated by law until 1923), so this is not a spelling variant — it names a different father.

**Same-person score: 0.82** — strong algorithmically, driven by the matching given name, birth year, and place. However, the patronymic conflict is a core identifier conflict that caps the link at **speculative**, regardless of the score.

**Match assessment: Speculative.** The birth year and place fit perfectly, but the patronymic names a different father from what the tree attests. The link cannot exceed `speculative` unless the discrepancy can be explained (e.g., the census enumerator recorded the wrong patronymic, or Hans Olsen was known by a different name).

---

**Action needed from you:** The subagent is awaiting your confirmation before creating the link. Your options are:

dimensions.rationale: No new persons needed to be minted; all five census personas matched existing tree persons (I1–I5). The materialize_facts call enriched the existing persons with sourced facts (residence facts for 1870 and 1880, birth facts from census data). All facts carry source references (S10 for 1870, S11 for 1880) with quality ratings. No edges needed to be written because the skill did not mint new persons; the household relationships (parent-child, spouse) already exist in the tree (R1–R7). The scenario is a household record (census), so edges are owed only if new persons are minted, which did not occur. No person was overwritten or renamed to force a match.

dimensions.name: Score discipline
dimensions.rationale: same_person was invoked for every assertion with a tree candidate (a_001–a_020), regardless of provenance (all from record_read). The score (0.78, confidence 4) was recorded in match_score and informed the rationale but did not override the geographic-cap rule. The skill correctly treated the high score as supporting evidence for the qualitative match while capping confidence at `probable` due to the unexplained move. For relationship assertions (a_019, a_020), the second party (head) was scored separately with recordRole specified, not reused from the first party's persona. No score was inverted or treated as a verdict.
